faq.title: What is Signal's Sealed Sender protocol?
faq.description: In traditional encrypted messaging (like WhatsApp or iMessage), the server needs to know who is sending the message in order to authenticate the user and prevent spam. Signal's Sealed Sender protocol cryptographically encrypts the sender's identity inside an envelope that only the recipient can decrypt. Signal's servers deliver the message without knowing who sent it!

faq.title: Can Signal's servers see who is inside a Signal Private Group?
faq.description: No! In Signal Private Groups v2, group membership lists, group names, and avatars are stored on Signal's servers as cryptographically blinded ciphertext. The server uses verifiable secret sharing and anonymous zero-knowledge group credentials to route messages without ever knowing who belongs to the group.

faq.title: What happens if a subpoena is served on Signal for my group messages?
faq.description: Because Signal stores zero plaintext message logs, zero group rosters, and blinds sender metadata via Sealed Sender, Signal can only provide two data points to law enforcement: the Unix timestamp when an account was created, and the date of the last connection to Signal's servers.

html:
In modern digital surveillance, intelligence agencies and corporate data brokers frequently repeat a sobering operational truth: "We kill people based on metadata." (Former NSA Director Michael Hayden). While end-to-end encryption (E2EE) prevents an adversary from reading the plaintext contents of your messages, traditional communication protocols leak catastrophic amounts of Metadata: who you communicate with, at what exact timestamps, how frequently, and from what geographic network locations.

If an adversary knows that you messaged an oncologist, a bankruptcy attorney, or a whistleblower hotline at 2:00 AM, they do not need to read the words to deduce the intimate realities of your life. Signal fundamentally revolutionizes messaging privacy not merely by encrypting message content, but by systematically eradicating metadata through two breakthrough cryptographic architectures: the Sealed Sender Protocol and Private Groups v2.

The Metadata Problem in Traditional Messaging

To understand why Sealed Sender is revolutionary, examine how traditional end-to-end encrypted messaging services (such as WhatsApp, Telegram Secret Chats, or iMessage) operate:

  1. Alice writes a message to Bob. Alice's client encrypts the message payload using Bob's public key.
  2. To send the ciphertext across the network, Alice connects to the central server and presents her authentication token: "Hello Server, I am Alice. Please deliver this encrypted packet to Bob."
  3. The server cannot read the ciphertext, but it records an immutable database log: {timestamp: 1718029200, sender: Alice, recipient: Bob, payload_size: 1420_bytes}.

Over months of communication, the server constructs a complete, detailed Social Interaction Graph mapping every personal and professional relationship in Alice's life. When governments issue national security letters or subpoenas, the messaging provider is legally forced to surrender these relational communication logs.

How Signal's Sealed Sender Protocol Blinds the Server

Signal's Sealed Sender protocol dismantles the sender-recipient metadata connection by removing the sender's identity from the transport layer entirely. In Sealed Sender:

  • When Alice connects to the Signal server to send a message to Bob, she does NOT authenticate as Alice.
  • The server sees only an anonymous connection delivering an encrypted sealed envelope addressed to Bob.
  • The server literally cannot see who sent the packet! It dutifully drops the envelope into Bob's recipient queue without recording a sender identity.

The Cryptographic Mechanics of the Sealed Envelope

How can a server deliver a message without knowing who sent it, while simultaneously preventing spammers from flooding the network with anonymous junk? The answer lies in Short-Lived Sender Certificates:

  1. Certificate Issuance: When Alice registers or logs into Signal, the server issues her a short-lived Sender Certificate. This certificate cryptographically attests: "The bearer of this certificate is a valid, unbanned Signal user with phone number/UUID X, authorized to send messages on day Y."
  2. Envelope Packaging: When Alice messages Bob, she packages her plaintext message, her ephemeral public ratchet key, AND her Sender Certificate inside an encrypted inner envelope, encrypted using Bob's Identity Key.
  3. Delivery: Alice wraps the inner envelope in an outer delivery layer addressed solely to Bob's UUID. She transmits the packet to the server over an unauthenticated TLS connection.
  4. Unsealing: The server routes the envelope to Bob. Bob's phone receives the packet, uses Bob's private key to decrypt the inner envelope, unpacks Alice's Sender Certificate, verifies the cryptographic signature from Signal, and displays Alice's name and message on screen!

At no point in this entire transaction did Signal's servers know that Alice was communicating with Bob. If a court orders Signal to surrender logs of who messaged Bob, Signal can honestly state that such logs do not exist in the laws of physics!

Private Groups v2: Zero-Knowledge Group Architecture

In traditional messaging apps, group chats are managed by server-side databases: the server maintains a table of group names, group profile avatars, and lists of all member phone numbers. If an admin removes a user, the server updates the database row.

Signal's Private Groups v2 replaces server-side rosters with Verifiable Secret Sharing and Zero-Knowledge Anonymous Credentials:

  • Blinded Master Keys: When a group is created, a random 256-bit Group Master Key is generated on the creator's device. From this key, clients derive a Group Identifier, a Profile Key, and an Authorization Key.
  • Encrypted Group State: The group name, description, avatar, and roster of member UUIDs are encrypted using the Profile Key and stored on Signal's servers as an opaque blob of ciphertext. Signal's servers cannot read the group name, cannot see the avatar, and cannot determine how many members belong to the group!
  • Zero-Knowledge Access Tokens: When a member needs to post a message or invite a friend, they do not ask the server for permission. They generate a Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZK credential) derived from the Group Master Key. The server cryptographically verifies that the user possesses a valid membership token without learning who the user is or which group they belong to!

Configuring Sealed Sender for Anyone (Advanced Security)

By default, Signal enables Sealed Sender for all communications between established mutual contacts. However, if a stranger or new contact messages you, the server requires sender authentication to prevent spam floods.

Power users, journalists, and activists can configure Signal to accept Sealed Sender packets from any user on Earth:

  1. Open Signal on your mobile device.
  2. Tap your profile avatar in the top corner to open Settings.
  3. Navigate to Privacy.
  4. Scroll down to the Sealed Sender section.
  5. Toggle on Allow from anyone.
  6. (Optional) Toggle on Display indicators. Signal will display a small two-line sealed envelope icon next to message status timestamps, confirming that the message traversed the network with zero sender metadata!

Subpoena Auditing: What Signal Actually Yields to Governments

Signal's cryptographic architecture has been tested extensively in real-world criminal trials, grand jury subpoenas, and foreign court orders across the United States, Europe, and Australia. In every public court filing, Signal's legal response to federal subpoenas for user records has remained identical:

"Signal does not store user message content, group memberships, contact lists, call logs, location records, or communication metadata. The only information Signal can provide is the date and time an account was registered, and the date of the account's last connection to the service."

By shifting trust from corporate promises to mathematical and cryptographic guarantees, Signal remains the gold standard for global digital communication privacy.

Signal Secure Value Recovery (SVR) and Intel SGX Enclaves

A classic dilemma in encrypted communications is: What happens if you lose your phone or switch devices? In traditional systems, you lose your contact list, or the server stores your contacts in plaintext. Signal solved this using Secure Value Recovery (SVR) running inside hardware Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions) Enclaves:

  • Client-Side Master Key Derivation: When you set a 4-to-8-digit Signal PIN, your device uses Argon2id key stretching to generate an encryption key. Your contacts and profile keys are encrypted locally before leaving the phone.
  • Hardware-Enclaved Rate Limiting: The encrypted blob is stored in an Intel SGX enclave on Signal's cloud infrastructure. The enclave's hardware code strictly limits PIN guessing attempts to prevent brute-force attacks: if someone attempts more than a handful of wrong PINs, the enclave permanently cryptographically shreds the data! Because the code runs inside isolated hardware memory that even Signal's server administrators cannot read or modify, your contacts remain completely private.

Private Contact Discovery: Cryptographic Intersection Without Disclosure

When you install Signal, the app tells you which of your friends are already on Signal—without ever revealing your address book to Signal's servers! This is achieved via Private Contact Discovery:

  1. Your device hashes all phone numbers in your address book using a truncated cryptographic hash.
  2. The client connects to a verified Intel SGX hardware enclave on the server over a remote-attested secure channel.
  3. The enclave performs an in-memory set intersection with the global directory of registered Signal numbers, returning only the mutual matches.
  4. The enclave discards the contact hashes immediately. Signal's persistent databases never learn who is in your phone's address book!

Post-Quantum Cryptography: The PQXDH Protocol Transition

To defend encrypted communications against the future threat of quantum supercomputers running Shor's algorithm (which will break classical RSA and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman), Signal upgraded its key agreement protocol to PQXDH (Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman).

PQXDH creates a hybrid cryptographic handshake: combining classical Curve25519 elliptic curve keys with the post-quantum lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism CRYSTALS-Kyber-1024 (standardized by NIST as ML-KEM). Even if an adversary intercepts and archives encrypted Signal traffic today ("Harvest Now, Decrypt Later"), future quantum supercomputers will remain mathematically incapable of decrypting the communication!

Username Privacy: Decoupling Phone Numbers from Messaging

Historically, connecting with someone on Signal required sharing your real-world mobile phone number. To protect personal identities for activists, whistleblowers, and public figures, Signal engineered Cryptographic Usernames:

  • A Signal username is not a public profile handle displayed in a global directory; it is an ephemeral contact initiation token.
  • Under the hood, usernames are stored as 96-bit cryptographic hashes. The server routes initial connection requests using the hash without associating your mobile phone number with the recipient.
  • Users can configure phone number discovery to "Nobody", ensuring that strangers who have your phone number in their contact list cannot discover whether you possess an active Signal account.
